intro: The Ketuvim, the Writings, are the third and most varied part of the Tanakh. This unit reads five of its books closely: Psalms, the Song of Songs, Job, Ecclesiastes and Esther. Two of them are poetry from beginning to end. One is a poem of argument set inside a story. One is a speech about what lasts. One is a court tale that never mentions God. Together they show what the Writings do that the Torah and the Prophets do not: they let the people talk back.

The first chapter teaches how Hebrew poetry works. It has no rhyme and no fixed meter. It works by parallelism, a second line that answers the first, and by images, alphabets and the turn in the middle of a lament. You will read Psalms 23, 90, 137 and 150 in the Jewish Publication Society translation of 1917, see how the Song of Songs praises a beloved, and learn why Rabbi Akiva called that book the holy of holies. Then you will try the form yourself.

The second chapter reads three books that refuse easy answers. Job asks why the innocent suffer. Ecclesiastes calls everything breath and then tells you to enjoy your bread. Esther makes a room full of costumes laugh and then, in chapter 9, asks something harder. You will meet the rabbis who argued about whether these books belonged in Scripture, the commentators who read them, and the holidays on which they are still chanted. By the end you should be able to read a passage of Hebrew poetry, name what its lines are doing, and argue from the text about how its readers have understood it.
bigQuestion: How do the poems and hard books of the Writings let readers argue with suffering, time and power, and why did Jewish tradition keep them?

timeline.t: David, whom tradition links with many psalms, rules in Jerusalem
Babylon burns the Temple; the setting of Psalm 137 and Lamentations
Xerxes I rules Persia; most scholars identify him with Esther's Ahasuerus
Scholars date Job, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs to the Persian and early Greek periods (BCE)
Greek translation of the Torah begins; the Greek Esther later adds prayers naming God
Rabbi Akiva, as the Mishnah reports, calls the Song of Songs the holy of holies
The Mishnah is compiled, recording debates over Ecclesiastes and the Song
The Babylonian Talmud takes shape, with its debates on Job and Purim
Rashi writes commentaries on the Psalms, the Song and the Megillot
Maimonides finishes the Guide of the Perplexed, reading Job as a parable
Robert Lowth publishes his lectures naming parallelism in Hebrew poetry
The Jewish Publication Society publishes its English Tanakh, this course's text

words.d: the pairing of lines by meaning that is the basic pattern of Hebrew poetry
a poem whose lines or stanzas follow the 22 letters of the Hebrew alphabet in order
a psalm of complaint and plea that usually turns to trust or praise
Psalms 113-118, recited on festivals, the new moon and at the seder
the five scrolls read on holidays: Song of Songs, Ruth, Lamentations, Ecclesiastes, Esther
reading a surface story as standing for a deeper one, as Jewish tradition reads the Song of Songs
the view of Job's friends that suffering is punishment and prosperity reward
the storm from which God answers Job with questions about creation (Job 38-41)
a parable; the Talmud records the view that Job is a mashal and never lived
breath or vapor, the key word of Ecclesiastes, rendered vanity in JPS 1917
the holiday of lots on the fourteenth of Adar, when the scroll of Esther is read
a dispute; an argument for the sake of heaven, which Pirkei Avot says endures

test.q: What did Robert Lowth identify in 1753 as the basic unit of Hebrew poetry?
test.why: Lowth's lectures named parallelism, the pairing of lines by meaning, as the pattern behind Hebrew verse.

test.q: "A soft answer turneth away wrath; but a grievous word stirreth up anger" (Proverbs 15:1) is which kind of parallelism?
test.why: The second line states the opposite of the first, the contrast form Proverbs favors.

test.q: How many verses does Psalm 119 have, and why?
choices: 176, eight per letter of the 22-letter alphabet
test.why: Psalm 119 has 22 stanzas of 8 verses each, every verse in a stanza beginning with the same letter.
Psalm 90, opening Book 4, is headed "A Prayer of Moses the man of God."

test.q: What is the turn in a lament?
choices: The point where complaint becomes trust or praise
The last letter of the alphabet
The change from Hebrew to Aramaic
test.why: Laments like Psalm 13 move from complaint and plea to a sudden declaration of trust.

test.q: According to the Mishnah, what did Rabbi Akiva call the Song of Songs?
test.why: Mishnah Yadayim 3:5 reports Akiva saying all the Writings are holy but the Song is the holy of holies.

test.q: In the traditional Jewish allegorical reading of the Song of Songs, the woman stands for whom?
test.why: The Targum, midrash and Rashi read the woman as Israel and the man as God.

test.q: Which set of psalms is recited on festivals and at the Passover seder?
test.why: Hallel is Psalms 113 to 118, recited on festivals and the new moon.

test.q: How is the book of Job structured?
choices: A prose frame around a long poetic dialogue
test.why: Chapters 1-2 and the end of 42 are prose; chapters 3 to 42:6 are poetry.

test.q: What does God say about Job's friends in Job 42:7?
choices: That they have not spoken rightly of God, as Job has
test.why: The epilogue reverses the friends' theology by declaring that Job, not they, spoke rightly.

test.q: Which reader argued in the Guide of the Perplexed that Job is a parable about providence?
test.why: Maimonides, Guide 3:22-23, reads Job as a mashal whose speakers hold different views of how God governs.

test.q: What does the Hebrew word hevel, the key word of Ecclesiastes, literally mean?
test.why: Hevel is breath or mist; JPS 1917 renders it vanity, NJPS futility, Alter mere breath.

test.q: Why, according to Shabbat 30b, did the sages keep Ecclesiastes instead of hiding it?
choices: Because its beginning and end are words of Torah
Because it is read on Purim
test.why: The Talmud says the book's contradictions troubled the sages, but its first and last words are Torah.

test.q: Which of these is true of the Hebrew book of Esther?
test.why: The Hebrew text has no divine name; the Greek version adds prayers that do.

test.q: What is the source of the noise at Haman's name during the Megillah reading?
choices: Deuteronomy 25:19, the command to blot out Amalek, to whom Haman is linked
test.why: Haman the Agagite is tied to Amalek's king Agag, and the noise enacts the command to blot out Amalek's memory.

write.prompt: Does the Tanakh think the world is fair? Argue from Job 42:7, Ecclesiastes 3:9 or 9:7, and Esther 4:14. Say what each passage says and how at least two readers (the friends, the Talmud, Maimonides, Rashi, a modern scholar) have read it.
tips: Name the book, chapter and verse for every passage you cite, and the translation (JPS 1917).
Attribute every reading: the Talmud says, Maimonides argues, a literary reader notes. Never say what the text simply means.
Compare readings rather than ranking them. Show what question each reader is asking.
Use the unit's terms: parallelism, retribution theology, hevel, reversal, machloket.
End with your own position and the strongest objection to it from one of the readers you named.
